title: AI for Home Service Businesses
summary: An implementation plan for turning job records into better closeout packages, estimate checks, and callback analysis.
problem: A home service company can finish the field work and still lose hours assembling photos, reconciling scope, and answering questions about what happened on site. The first AI project should improve the record around a job, with dispatchers and technicians retaining operational decisions.
deliverable: A reviewed job closeout packet tied to a work-order ID
inputs: Approved work order, technician notes, completion photos with descriptions, signed changes, and the company’s closeout checklist.
workflows: Job closeout assembly
Group notes and photo references by the approved scope; list missing completion evidence.
Technician or supervisor confirms the work actually performed.
Minutes from completed work to an accepted packet.
Estimate scope comparison
Compare a draft estimate with the inspection notes and required scope fields.
Estimator approves quantities, labor assumptions, and exclusions.
Estimates returned for missing scope.
Callback pattern review
Group completed callback records by documented issue, equipment, and original job.
Service manager verifies causes before changing training or process.
Repeated callbacks for the same documented cause.
example: Illustrative case: a technician records that a replacement was recommended, while the signed work order only authorizes diagnosis. The closeout packet should distinguish the completed diagnostic work from the proposed replacement. It must not mark the replacement as completed or create an invoice line for it.
steps: Choose one service line with a consistent closeout checklist and a supervisor who can review the trial.
Collect completed jobs including a callback, a scope change, missing photos, and an incomplete technician note.
Generate packets in a separate draft area and reconcile each statement to the work-order evidence.
Track review and correction time alongside packet assembly time before changing the live process.
exceptions: Missing completion evidence, a customer dispute, an ambiguous technician note, or a proposed change outside signed scope should return to the responsible operator. AI should not determine whether a site is safe or direct a technician through hazardous work.
handoff: Keep the accepted packet, the work-order reference, a list of unresolved items, and the approving supervisor. Require a fresh review when scope changes.

title: AI for Marketing Agencies
summary: Build a campaign evidence and approval system that connects client inputs, creative versions, and publishing decisions.
problem: Agencies often have enough draft copy and too little clarity about which client facts, claims, and creative versions have been approved. A useful AI implementation makes evidence and approvals easy to inspect across a campaign.
deliverable: A campaign readiness packet with a claim ledger and versioned approvals
inputs: Signed campaign brief, approved client facts, brand guidance, creative drafts, distribution plan, and recorded client feedback.
workflows: Campaign evidence review
Map factual claims in each asset to supplied evidence and flag unsupported promises.
Account lead and client owner approve claims and permitted uses.
Assets returned for unsupported claims.
Cross-asset consistency
Compare offer details, dates, eligibility, and calls to action across campaign versions.
Campaign manager resolves conflicting source instructions.
Conflicting details caught before release.
Approval reconciliation
Match client feedback to the exact creative version and list unresolved comments.
Account lead confirms the final version authorized for each channel.
Time spent locating valid final approval.
example: Illustrative case: the client approves a landing page offering a consultation, then a social draft describes a guaranteed result. The readiness packet should identify the changed claim and leave the social asset unapproved. Approval of one asset does not authorize every derivative.
steps: Select one campaign with a named client approver and a stable set of source facts.
Assign a version ID to each asset and a source ID to every supporting claim.
Review the campaign packet together with the client rather than asking for a generic final signoff.
Keep publication controls separate until the exact asset and destination have been approved.
exceptions: Conflicting client instructions, missing claim support, licensed material without documented permission, and altered offers require an explicit resolution. Remove unnecessary customer information from research inputs.
handoff: Preserve the final assets, source ledger, approval versions, channel destinations, and any expiration dates on the offer. Make the next refresh owner visible.

title: AI for Property Management Operations
summary: Organize vendor closeouts, property document versions, and owner reporting with clear human review.
problem: Property managers need a reliable connection between a maintenance request, approved work, vendor evidence, and owner communication. AI can help assemble that chain while the manager retains authority over spending, access, and resident communication.
deliverable: A reviewed maintenance completion and owner-reporting bundle
inputs: Approved work orders, vendor completion notes, invoices, property identifiers, approved communication templates, and current operating procedures.
workflows: Vendor completion review
Match invoice line items and completion evidence to the authorized work order.
Property manager confirms completion and approves payment through the existing process.
Invoices needing a second evidence request.
Owner report assembly
Summarize approved work, open items, and source-linked spending records by property.
Portfolio manager checks totals and exclusions against accounting records.
Review minutes per accepted owner report.
Operating document control
Identify superseded inspection checklists and inconsistent vendor instructions.
Operations owner selects the authoritative procedure.
Incidents involving outdated instructions.
example: Illustrative case: a vendor’s invoice says a repair was completed, but the closeout note says a part is still on order. The bundle should show the conflict and leave the job open for a manager’s review rather than generate a completion notice.
steps: Pilot the bundle on completed maintenance work without changing resident intake or emergency handling.
Use property and work-order IDs so records from different buildings cannot be mixed by similar names.
Include a disputed invoice, partial completion, duplicate invoice, and changed authorization in the test set.
Review accepted bundles with the accounting and property teams before expanding portfolio coverage.
exceptions: Emergency requests follow the existing emergency process. Do not use these administrative workflows to screen residents, determine eligibility, interpret legal notices, or make housing decisions.
handoff: Record the property ID, authorized scope, evidence links, unresolved issues, and manager approval. Keep owner reporting permissions separate from vendor access.

title: AI for Business Acquisition Teams
summary: Build a traceable diligence question register and post-close operating handoff from a controlled deal room.
problem: A deal team can read a large volume of documents without resolving the questions that matter to the investment decision. An AI-assisted process should make contradictions and missing evidence easier to assign, verify, and close.
deliverable: An evidence-linked diligence issue register with a post-close handoff
inputs: An authorized deal-room index, dated seller responses, financial records selected by the finance lead, operating procedures, and the buyer’s diligence scope.
workflows: Diligence issue register
Match open questions to evidence, seller responses, and conflicting documents.
Diligence lead assigns severity and decides when an issue is resolved.
Open issues lacking an owner or evidence reference.
Seller knowledge handoff
Organize approved interview notes into operating dependencies and transition questions.
Incoming operating lead verifies the actual process with staff.
Critical processes with an accepted handoff.
Post-close dependency map
Connect transition actions to access, staff, supplier, and system prerequisites.
Integration owner approves dates and sequencing.
Blocked actions with an unresolved prerequisite.
example: Illustrative case: a seller presentation describes recurring contracts, while the supplied customer schedule includes month-to-month arrangements. The register should quote both sources and ask for reconciliation. It should not independently classify revenue quality or revise the purchase price.
steps: Define diligence workstreams and who can access each deal-room section.
Create a stable issue ID and require source references for each factual statement.
Test the workflow on an incomplete response, contradictory figures, a superseded file, and an unanswered question.
Export accepted unresolved issues into the first operating handoff while preserving their deal context.
exceptions: Valuation, legal interpretation, financing suitability, and investment approval remain with the responsible professionals. Treat seller claims as claims until supported by the required evidence.
handoff: Retain issue history, source versions, reviewer conclusions, and any conditions that must be met after signing or close. Restrict access as deal participants change.

title: AI for Professional Service Firms
summary: Design a scope-to-delivery system for consulting teams that keeps commitments, assumptions, and review responsibility visible.
problem: Professional service teams can lose margin when proposals, working notes, and client expectations describe different deliverables. The first implementation should connect an approved engagement to a clear delivery plan and a record of changes.
deliverable: An engagement scope and delivery evidence register
inputs: Signed scope, approved amendments, client intake, project assumptions, milestone definitions, and the firm’s deliverable review standards.
workflows: Scope-to-plan mapping
Map contracted deliverables to milestones, inputs, acceptance evidence, and a reviewer.
Engagement lead verifies that the plan reflects the signed scope.
Deliverables without a defined acceptance condition.
Change request preparation
Compare a new client request with the approved scope and draft clarification questions.
Engagement lead decides scope and commercial treatment.
Unplanned work started before scope clarification.
Deliverable readiness review
Check required sections and supplied evidence before a professional review.
Qualified reviewer owns the advice and final client deliverable.
Review cycles caused by incomplete preparation.
example: Illustrative case: the scope includes a diagnostic report and a client asks the team to implement every recommendation. The system should identify the request as a possible scope change and prepare a decision brief. It must not promise additional work or fees.
steps: Choose one repeatable engagement type with a clear written scope.
Build a mapping from deliverable to required client inputs and acceptance evidence.
Test a missing input, changed deadline, ambiguous deliverable, and additional client request.
Use accepted registers in a team handoff and compare clarification loops with the previous process.
exceptions: Client-specific legal, tax, medical, and financial conclusions require the appropriate qualified professional. These administrative systems do not establish professional compliance or authorize advice.
handoff: Store accepted scope mappings, open assumptions, approved amendments, and review assignments. Carry unresolved client dependencies into each status update.

title: AI for Ecommerce Operations
summary: Use AI to review catalog evidence, product changes, and return reasons without inventing product claims.
problem: An ecommerce operation needs consistent product information across listings, support answers, and internal records. AI is useful when it helps find discrepancies and prepare changes that a catalog owner can verify against supplier evidence.
deliverable: A catalog change and product-claim review queue
inputs: Approved supplier specifications, current catalog exports, product IDs, documented return reasons, and the business’s publication standards.
workflows: Specification discrepancy review
Compare live listing fields with the approved specification version.
Catalog owner validates the source and approves corrections.
Listing discrepancies resolved with source evidence.
Product claim preparation
Link proposed claims to specification passages and mark unsupported attributes.
Merchandising owner confirms permitted claims before publication.
Draft claims removed for missing support.
Return reason synthesis
Group documented return comments by product ID and issue without inferring unsupported defects.
Operations owner checks the records and selects investigation actions.
Return themes supported by traceable examples.
example: Illustrative case: a supplier sheet specifies indoor use, while a draft listing calls the product weatherproof. The queue should flag the unsupported claim and retain the original specification. Customer comments describing outdoor use do not establish a tested product capability.
steps: Pilot one product family with stable IDs and approved source specifications.
Separate observed listing differences from proposed replacement text.
Test variant mix-ups, missing measurements, conflicting sheets, and unsupported compatibility claims.
Publish only the catalog owner’s accepted changes and retain the prior listing version.
exceptions: Safety claims, regulated products, compatibility, warranty terms, and certification statements need the relevant source and reviewer. Do not infer them from similar listings or marketing language.
handoff: Keep the product ID, variant ID, source version, proposed field changes, approval, and publication outcome. Recheck support answers when the catalog changes.

title: AI for Nonprofit Operations
summary: Create a program evidence and reporting process that preserves the difference between activities, outputs, and measured outcomes.
problem: Nonprofits may have strong program records spread across notes, spreadsheets, and partner reports. An AI implementation can help assemble reporting evidence while keeping claims limited to what the organization actually measured.
deliverable: A program reporting evidence pack with unresolved measurement gaps
inputs: Approved program records, reporting definitions, grant requirements, consent and publication rules, and verified aggregate counts.
workflows: Requirement-to-evidence mapping
Match each reporting question to the approved records that address it.
Program lead confirms the evidence meets the reporting definition.
Report requirements with verified supporting records.
Activity and outcome separation
Distinguish services delivered from outcomes measured and assumptions made.
Measurement owner approves the interpretation.
Unsupported outcome statements caught in review.
Partner report reconciliation
Compare partner submissions for inconsistent periods, units, and duplicate activity counts.
Reporting owner resolves discrepancies before combining totals.
Reconciliation questions remaining at submission.
example: Illustrative case: a program logged 120 workshop attendances but did not track unique attendees or longer-term results. The report should describe attendances and the limits of the measurement. It should not claim 120 distinct people achieved a lasting outcome.
steps: Choose one recurring internal report and define the units and reporting period.
Use aggregate or appropriately de-identified records approved for the tool.
Test duplicate participation, missing dates, incompatible partner definitions, and an unmeasured outcome.
Have the program and reporting owners accept the evidence pack before using it in an external submission.
exceptions: Individual eligibility, assistance allocation, sensitive beneficiary stories, and unapproved personal information remain outside this administrative pilot. Confirm permitted uses before drafting a public narrative.
handoff: Preserve reporting definitions, verified counts, source references, known gaps, and the final approval. Carry measurement improvements into the next reporting cycle.

title: AI for Podcast and Media Teams
summary: Build an episode production system connecting transcripts, speaker verification, show notes, and reusable content.
problem: A media team can generate many clips and summaries from a recording while losing track of context, publication permissions, and corrected statements. A useful implementation preserves a clear relationship between the source episode and every derivative.
deliverable: An episode release pack with timestamped evidence and derivative approvals
inputs: Approved recording, corrected transcript, guest publication permissions, episode brief, fact-check notes, and channel requirements.
workflows: Episode evidence outline
Identify themes, claims needing verification, and relevant timestamps.
Producer confirms context and editorial treatment.
Claims unresolved before episode release.
Derivative content mapping
Draft clips, show notes, and article outlines tied to source passages.
Editor checks that each derivative preserves the speaker’s meaning.
Derivatives returned for context loss.
Correction propagation
Identify which published derivatives depend on a corrected episode statement.
Managing editor decides the correction and distribution steps.
Affected assets with a recorded correction action.
example: Illustrative case: a guest describes a failed experiment before explaining why it failed. A short clip containing only the original tactic would reverse the lesson. The release pack should preserve the qualifying passage or exclude that clip.
steps: Select one episode and create a corrected transcript with stable timestamps.
Map proposed assets to the exact passages they depend on.
Test a speaker correction, a disputed statistic, an off-record section, and a quote requiring nearby context.
Approve each destination asset and retain a dependency map for later corrections.
exceptions: Publication restrictions, licensed media, disputed factual claims, and sensitive guest information require editorial resolution. Do not fabricate quotations or attribute a generated statement to a speaker.
handoff: Store the accepted transcript, timestamps, permissions, asset versions, approvals, and live destinations. Assign an editor to manage corrections after publication.
